list.listitem: Thromboangiitis obliterans (TAO) is diagnosed clinically, typically in a young, male smoker with the characteristic presentation of distal extremity ischemia often affecting more than one limb and accompanied by migratory phlebitis and Raynaud's phenomenon. C
Exclude atherosclerosis and other causes of vasculitis by laboratory tests and angiography. C
Disease remission to avoid amputation by tobacco cessation is the primary therapeutic goal. B
IV iloprost relieves pain (NNT = 7) and healing, while oral iloprost may not. B

background.definition: TAO, or Buerger's disease, is an inflammatory disease of the small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities characterized by segmental thrombotic occlusion.

list.listitem: Prevalence reported in 1986 was at 13 per 100,000 patients.
TAO is more common in men.
While tobacco use appears to play a critical role in the etiology, an exact cause is not known.
An autoimmune etiology is suggested by the presence of elevated levels of antiendothelial cell antibodies in patients with active disease.

The pathophysiologic process is distinct from atherosclerosis, an idea first proposed by Buerger, who demonstrated by histopathology the origin of the pathology in an obliterating thrombus, and a distal to proximal disease progression.
Identification of cell types in arterial lesions by immunohistochemical means suggests a T-cell and B-cell mediated endarteritis.
Impairment in the endothelial-dependent vasodilation of peripheral vessels may have a role.

Early changes include occlusive thrombus development in arteries and veins with sparing of the vessel wall. Thrombus organization and nonspecific fibrosis is seen in chronic disease. Large proximal and visceral vessels are typically spared.
Findings consistent with inflammation of distal small- to medium-sized arteries and veins in a young, male smoker are presumptive for TAO. C
Diagnosis is by generally accepted clinical criteria when other causes of vasculitis are excluded. C
Nonspecific angiographic findings may support the clinical diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Large, proximal vessel involvement, relatively older age of onset, and presence of typical risk factors

list.listitem: A typical presentation is foot or leg claudication, a manifestation of infrapopliteal, such as posterior tibial, or plantar arterial occlusion. The average age of initial symptoms is 34 years, with diagnosis 10 years later.

Ischemic ulcerations of the upper extremities alone were present in 21% of patients, of the lower extremity alone in 35% of patients, and of both the upper and lower extremities in 20% of patients in 1 series.
Thrombophlebitis occurred in 43% of patients in a study of 255 patients in Japan.
Raynaud's phenomenon was found in 44% of patients in 1 study. A recent meta-analysis found the prevalence to be closer to 30%.
Positive findings on the Allen test in a patient presenting with only lower extremity symptoms, although not specific for TAO, may be indicative of asymptomatic upper extremity involvement.
No specific tests are available to diagnosis TAO. Laboratory tests are employed to identify risk factors for atherosclerosis and to identify and exclude other causes of vasculitis.

Recommended tests include blood count, chemistry profile, fasting blood glucose, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, serologic markers for disorders associated with small vessel vasculitis (eg, CREST and scleroderma), and a hypercoagulability battery.
Echocardiography and arteriography are suggested to evaluate for a proximal embolic source.
Arteriographic findings of segmental occlusive lesions of small and medium vessels, "corkscrew" collateral vessels, and proximal arteries free of disease are suggestive but not diagnostic of TAO.
A scoring system that aids in defining disease probability has been proposed and found to be useful.

Factors in the score that increase the likelihood of TAO include younger age, intermittent claudication, upper extremity symptoms, male gender, migrating superficial vein thrombosis, and the presence of Raynaud's phenomenon.
TAO should be suspected in the young, male smoker who presents with distal extremity ischemia.

No specific test identifies the disease; rather, diagnosis is based on the following clinical criteria: age at onset less than 45 to 50 years, smoking history, infrapopliteal arterial occlusion with sparing of proximal vessels, upper extremity involvement, migrating superficial thrombophlebitis, and the exclusion of other diseases or factors, including diabetes, hypercoagulable states, and arteriosclerosis.
Smoking cessation is the mainstay of therapy.
Tobacco cessation is the primary intervention associated with disease remission. B
IV iloprost relieves pain (NNT = 7) and healing, but oral iloprost may not. B
Autologous cell therapy appears effective in endpoints of ischemia, subjective symptoms, ulcer healing, and amputation. B
Measures including intramedullary Kirschner wire placement, implantable spinal cord stimulators, and gene therapy may heal ulcers and provide pain relief. C
Pneumatic compression of the extremity may promote ischemic ulcer healing. C

Oral iloprost 100 mcg twice daily was more effective than placebo at relieving rest pain (63% vs. 49%, NNT = 7) but was no more effective in healing ischemic ulcers at 6-month follow-up. A study of oral iloprost at doses of 50 to 100 mcg twice daily or 150 to 200 mcg twice daily compared with placebo over 1 year failed to demonstrate improvement in time before amputation or death, but found modest benefit for rest pain and need for analgesia at low and high doses for 23% and 26% of patients, respectively, compared to 18% for placebo.
IV therapy with iloprost was more effective than aspirin (response rate 88% vs. 21%, NNT = 2) for ulcer healing and pain relief after 6 months in a randomized double-blind trial.

A Cochrane review identified 5 RCTs with 602 patients. It concluded that IV iloprost was more effective than aspirin for pain and healing, but that oral iloprost was not more effective than placebo. There is no evidence of differing effectiveness between iloprost, clinprost, and alprostadil for pain and healing. Folic acid is not effective.

Sympathectomy may provide symptomatic improvement. However, in an RCT with 200 patients, IV iloprost was superior to lumbar sympathectomy for ulcer healing rate at 4 weeks (61.9% vs. 41%, NNT = 5) and 24 weeks (85.3% vs. 52.3%, NNT = 3). It was also superior for pain relief at both 4 and 24 weeks.
Arterial bypass surgery is limited due to the segmental pattern and distal focus of TAO. Limb salvage was achieved in reported cases despite poor patency rates.
Placement of an intramedullary Kirschner wire may reduce pain and facilitate ulcer healing by stimulating angiogenesis.

A systematic review identified 15 studies of endovascular therapy with 402 endovascular procedures. Critical ischemia was present in 92% and most lesions were below the knee. The technical success rate was 85%, and primary patency was 66% at 12 months and 51% at 3 years.
Smoking cessation is associated with the arrest of disease progression and symptom remission.
Amputation is significantly reduced or eliminated by discontinuation of tobacco use.
Implantable spinal cord stimulators are reported to provide pain control and improve perfusion and healing of ulcers.

In a meta-analysis of 37 trials, autologous cell therapy was effective in improving endpoints of ischemia, subjective symptoms, ulcer healing, and amputation; intramuscular administration and use of bone marrow cells appeared most effective. Patients with TAO showed some larger benefits than patients with atherosclerotic peripheral vascular disease.

Stem cell therapy is an area of investigation for this disease process. Stem cell injection with autologous peripheral blood CD133+ cells prevented amputation in 7 of 9 patients with critical limb ischemia and in 2 longer term case series (N = 42 and 123, respectively) peripheral blood mononuclear cell implantation improved ischemic symptoms with fewer amputations than expected; in the larger study the 1-year amputation-free rates were 70% to 83% and common serious adverse events included heart failure (15 cases), myocardial infarction (15 cases), serious infection (13 cases), stroke (10 cases), and malignant tumor (9 cases).
In another small case series using bone marrow derived stem cells, there was significant improvement in pain and walking distance with ulcer healing in 3 of 5 patients with severe Buerger's disease.
Investigational gene therapy with endothelial growth factor may improve healing and relieve pain.
In an observational study, ulcer healing was improved in patients treated by intermittent pneumatic compression.
In a series of 69 patients followed for 11 years, 54 required an average of 4 operations, with 40 undergoing 1 or more amputations. B
The rate of amputation is twofold higher in patients who continue to smoke. B
